entries.title: Ashoka Fellowship: Rolling Nominations for Systems-Changing Social Entrepreneurs
entries.sectors: Social entrepreneurship, systems change, social innovation and mission-driven enterprise
entries.summary: Ashoka accepts nominations and self-nominations for leading social entrepreneurs in active Fellowship countries. Ashoka East Africa serves Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and Tanzania, and the current recommendation form accepts self-nominations.
entries.support: Lifelong Fellowship network and tailored support; a stipend for up to three years may be offered when needed, but financial support is not automatic
entries.deadline_label: Rolling nominations; no fixed closing date is stated on the current Fellowship recommendation form
entries.countries: Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and Tanzania are served by Ashoka East Africa; the live form also lists active Fellowship countries globally.
benefits: A lifelong Fellowship community with peer connections, visibility and tailored engagement support for selected Fellows.
Ashoka states that a tailored stipend for up to three years may be provided when needed so a Fellow can focus full-time on the idea; not every Fellow receives financial support.
Access to Ashoka's regional and global network after completing its multi-stage selection process.
eligibility: A social entrepreneur with a genuinely new idea or approach capable of changing a pattern or system, rather than only delivering a conventional local service.
The founder or co-founder should demonstrate entrepreneurial quality, social impact, ethical fibre and potential for large-scale systems change under Ashoka's published selection criteria.
Applicants can self-nominate through the recommendation form, but the nomination begins a rigorous local and global selection process and is not a direct award application.
conditions: Ashoka does not promise a fixed grant amount and states that financial support depends on the Fellow's needs.
Selected Fellows are expected to give priority to the work for which they are elected and, under current guidance, commit full-time to advancing the idea.
A nomination does not guarantee an interview or election; Ashoka may archive nominations from countries where Fellowship activity is not currently open.
steps: Read Ashoka's Fellowship criteria and selection process before submitting a nomination.
Prepare concise evidence of the social problem, what is genuinely new about the solution, the current scale of impact and the strategy for changing the wider system.
Use the official Ashoka Fellowship recommendation form and select self-nomination if applying for your own work.
entries.notice: This is a nomination and selection process, not a standard cash-grant call. A stipend is needs-based and is not guaranteed to every Fellow.

guide.context: The Ashoka Fellowship is designed for social entrepreneurs whose work aims to change a system rather than simply expand a service. In East Africa, Ashoka maintains an active regional Fellowship across Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and Tanzania. The current public form explicitly allows a social entrepreneur to nominate themselves, which means a founder does not need to wait for an outside nominator before entering the first stage.
guide.fit: A strong fit is a founder who has already moved beyond a purely conceptual idea and can show evidence that a distinctive approach is changing behaviour, institutions, markets, policy or another underlying pattern. An early pilot with little evidence, a local service that simply duplicates an existing model, or a founder who cannot commit deeply to the work is less likely to match Ashoka's stated criteria.
prepare: Write a one-paragraph explanation of the root social problem and why existing approaches have not solved it.
Describe the core idea in a way that makes its novelty and systems-change logic visible without exaggerating results.
Prepare credible evidence of impact to date, replication or influence, and the founder's own role in building and scaling the work.
guide.strategy: Treat the nomination as a systems-change case, not a conventional funding pitch. The strongest evidence should show how the idea changes incentives, practices, relationships or institutions beyond the organisation's direct beneficiaries. Be specific about what is already happening, what remains a hypothesis and how the approach could spread independently. If the organisation also earns revenue, explain how the economic model supports the social mission without implying that revenue alone proves systemic impact.
guide.commitment: Ashoka's selection process includes local review, interviews, reference and background checks, an external second-opinion review, a regional selection panel and final Board review. That can take substantial time. The Fellowship is lifelong, while any stipend is needs-based rather than automatic. Do not build a financial plan around an assumed stipend before election. Confirm current country activity and form instructions immediately before submitting.

entries.title: ILO Safe Labour Migration Competitions 2026: Essays, Research and Storytelling
entries.organisation: International Labour Organization (ILO) / Better Regional Migration Management Programme
entries.sectors: Labour migration, decent work, research, journalism, media, public policy and youth
entries.summary: The ILO has opened three competitions for university students, researchers, journalists and media creators from seven East and Horn of Africa countries, including Kenya, on safe, regular and orderly labour migration.
entries.support: First-place winners are invited to the Fifth Labour Migration Advisory Group meeting in Zanzibar, 16–18 December 2026, with travel and accommodation covered by the ILO
entries.deadline_label: 25 November 2026; the ILO announcement states the date but does not specify a cutoff time
entries.countries: Djibouti, Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, South Sudan, Tanzania and Uganda
benefits: Three entry tracks: a university essay competition, a research paper competition and a journalism/storytelling competition.
First-place winners are invited to participate in the Fifth Labour Migration Advisory Group meeting in Zanzibar from 16 to 18 December 2026.
The ILO states that travel and accommodation for first-place winners attending the Zanzibar meeting will be covered.
eligibility: University students can enter the Young Voices on Safe Migration for Work essay track.
Academics, researchers and doctoral candidates can enter the research paper competition.
Journalists, photographers, filmmakers and content creators can enter the journalism and storytelling track, subject to the detailed competition guidelines.
conditions: Applicants must be from one of the seven listed countries and follow the detailed track-specific eligibility and submission rules.
The public ILO announcement gives a 25 November 2026 deadline but does not state a time of day, so applicants should not assume they can submit late on the deadline date.
Travel and accommodation support described by the ILO applies to first-place winners invited to the December meeting; it should not be assumed for every entrant.
steps: Choose the appropriate essay, research or journalism/storytelling track and read the linked ILO guidelines for that track.
Prepare an original submission on safe, regular and orderly labour migration, using the format and evidence requirements in the official guidelines.
Submit using the route specified in the ILO competition guidance well before 25 November because no cutoff time is stated in the public announcement.
sources: ILO launch announcement and competition links
entries.notice: The ILO announcement links separate detailed guidelines for the three tracks. Read the relevant track guidance before submitting; this listing does not invent a deadline time or requirements that are not stated publicly.

guide.context: The ILO's Better Regional Migration Management programme is using three writing and media competitions to bring student, research and public-interest storytelling perspectives into regional labour-migration discussions. For Kenyan applicants, the opportunity is not a startup grant or enterprise accelerator. It is a content and research competition connected to a regional policy meeting on worker protection and safe migration.
guide.fit: The opportunity is strongest for a student, academic, doctoral researcher, journalist, photographer, filmmaker or content creator who already has a credible connection to labour, migration, employment, worker rights, recruitment, reintegration or related public-policy questions. A business founder should apply only if they genuinely fit one of the stated participant categories and can produce the required original work.
prepare: Select the correct track first; the essay, research and storytelling competitions have different audiences and expected formats.
Use reliable evidence and avoid sensational claims about migrant workers, irregular migration or recruitment practices.
Plan to finish before the published date because the public announcement does not give a closing hour or timezone.
guide.strategy: A strong submission should add a useful perspective rather than merely repeat general statements about migration. For a research paper, connect evidence to a clear policy or implementation question. For journalism or storytelling, centre accurate and responsible representation of migrant workers' experiences. For the student essay, develop a coherent argument grounded in decent work and fair recruitment. Follow the official track guidance where it differs from this editorial preparation advice.
guide.commitment: The public announcement says first-place winners will be invited to Zanzibar for the Fifth Labour Migration Advisory Group meeting from 16 to 18 December 2026 and that the ILO will cover travel and accommodation for those winners. Do not assume a cash prize, visa support beyond what is stated, or travel funding for non-winners. Retain proof of submission and be available for the December meeting if selected.
